question: How does the old Érard carry the étude’s contrasting touches?
intro: Martha Goldstein plays an Érard piano dated 1851 in this recording from the Al Goldstein collection. The instrument’s date is documented; the session date is not, so this is an instrument comparison rather than a dated nineteenth-century performance.

cues.title: The instrument, not the session
cues.text: The source identifies an Érard piano from 1851 and Martha Goldstein as performer. It gives no recording date: the age of the instrument must not be mistaken for the age of the performance.
cues.evidence: Commons recording description: “Martha Goldstein, Piano (Erard, 1851)”; the Date field is blank.

cues.title: Weight after a quieter passage
cues.text: The central continuation gains weight after a quieter stretch. Compare the tone’s decay and the line between attacks with Neeman’s performance, allowing for the different recording conditions.
cues.evidence: A 0:58 boundary follows the low 0:50–0:55 windows at −24 dB; 1:00 rises to −15.5 dB. The source establishes the instrument, not microphone conditions.

cues.title: A later change of surface
cues.text: The later stretch becomes more active after a quiet preparation. Follow the changing touch while keeping the melodic outline recognisable.
cues.evidence: The 2:06 boundary lies between −21.4 dB at 2:05 and a stronger 2:15 window; detected attacks rise from 1.4 at 2:00 to 3.8 at 2:10.

cues.title: A final measured crest
cues.text: The closing gestures reach the strongest recorded window of this performance before the sound falls away. Compare the spacing around that crest rather than judging the instrument only by its brightest notes.
cues.evidence: The largest boundary is 2:44, followed by the loudest relative-level window at 2:50, −10.7 dB. The level falls to −27.7 at 3:00 and −73.4 at 3:05.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
